The House of Romanov. Ruling Russia for over three centuries from 1613 to 1918, the Romanovs transformed it from a provincial Muscovite state into one of the world's largest and most powerful empires. Under towering figures like Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, they modernized Russia, expanded its territories across three continents, and made it a major player in European power politics.

Michael Romanov was elected Tsar in 1613 after the chaos of the Time of Troubles. Peter the Great reigned from 1682 to 1725 and westernized Russia. He built the city of Saint Petersburg as a window to the West and modernized the military. He even visited Western Europe incognito to learn. Catherine the Great reigned from 1762 to 1796 as an enlightened despot. She expanded Russian territory through wars with the Ottoman Empire and Poland, making Russia a great power.

The Romanovs ruled an autocracy where the Tsar was the supreme authority. A centralized bureaucracy and military were instruments of imperial control. They expanded Russian territory from Eastern Europe to Siberia and the Pacific, controlling vast multiethnic domains of Slavs, Caucasians, Central Asians, and others. Nicholas II reigned from 1894 to 1917 as the last Tsar. He faced revolution born of modernization, war defeats in the Russo-Japanese War and World War I, and mounting social unrest. He abdicated in March 1917. The family was executed by Bolsheviks in July 1918, ending the dynasty and any hope of restoration.
